title: Playing melody and phrasing: Hodges, Ray Charles, Parker
summary: Henry's straight Misty won a standing ovation; Durham says melody phrased well wins the public, citing Hodges, Armstrong and Ray Charles, against Parker's showmanship.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Well, the thing is, when I said they can't play melody, well, they can play melody, but what they don't know anymore is how to phrase it, so that it has -- you know, they don't give it any expression.
Yeah, but Henry came out there and he played "Misty" on his soprano. He didn't put an extra note in it and he got a standing ovation. The house was packed.
What was he doing in Kansas City?
No, he came out (inaudible).
Oh, I thought it was --

One weekend on his vacation, brought his wife. Hal Austin told him to come as a guest and he had the hotel as a guest, you know. So he came out and they gave him a suite, gave him all he want to eat. He wanted to play. That's why he was out there. So (inaudible) got his picture all in the paper, the whole page, two or three of them, two or three different pages out there. You ought to see his write-ups.
Well, that's very good.
He liked that, you know?
Sure.
But he played "Misty." He just broke up the house. He didn't play an extra note on the melody. He (inaudible) and then he played "Sophisticated Lady" on his
baritone, did the same thing. Had to play it over again. Just nothing but melody.
Well, I mean --
(Inaudible) that melody. Louie Armstrong say that he has a (inaudible) and you get offstage, close to that melody as you can, and the public will get with you. The musicians may not like it.
(Laughter.)
Well, I mean, I certainly don't want to hear somebody just play melody without any sort of taste or anything, but --
You got to have an awful taste.
Hm?
To do that, you got to have an awful taste with it.
But it's how you phrase it, isn't it?
Yeah.
I mean, that's the important thing. You know, you ruin any tune, if you don't phrase it properly.
Got to really phrase it.
Yeah.
You got to play it like you sing it.
But that's what they don't know, you see?
You ever heard anybody phrase like Johnny Hodges?
Well, yeah, there you go.
Look like he's coming a mile before he hit the note.
(Laughter.)
Yeah.
And then he run a few little extras in the places. Sometime (inaudible) next one in Georgia.
Well, you take --
But I saw I had the public with the melody.
Yeah.
You know, in the way I was playing the melody. So how many _________ can Ray Charles do when he sings (inaudible)? How much running can he do? But he breaks up the house, doesn't he?
That's right.
See, you got to learn how to play a melody, phrase it.

But of course, you know, when you bring a Johnny Hodges, this is where the Charlie Parker thing -- that influenced the whole generation of musicians and I mean, what Johnny stood for, that's really been lost anyway.
Well, what Johnny did, he played for the
public, for the people.
Yeah, but there was a lot of feeling in that.
That's what I say. Charlie (inaudible) showmanship. He can't remember a note he played.
(Recording interruption.)
